title: JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (Dec 2022 TCC) Case
subject: SR&ED dispute involving product development and whether the taxpayer proved technological advancement and eligible expenditures.
keyPhrase: JEC Distributors v The King 2022 TCC
summary: JEC Distributors v. The King (2022 TCC 170) shows how Canadian SR&ED claims fail without objective proof of technological uncertainty. On December 28, 2022, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed the Toronto-heard appeal of a welding-products manufacturer whose $91,537 claim for three projects was denied, holding that subjective inability to solve problems does not establish uncertainty beyond routine engineering.
metaDescription: Analyze the December 2022 Tax Court of Canada ruling in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King on Canadian SR&ED tax credit compliance.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Dispute and Procedural Posture

On December 28, 2022, the Tax Court of Canada rendered its judgment in JEC Distributors Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2022 TCC 170, dismissing the corporate taxpayer's appeal from the reassessment of its taxation year ending September 30, 2016, under which the Minister of National Revenue had denied its claim for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures of $91,537 relating to three projects. The Appellant, JEC Distributors Inc., is described by the Court as a manufacturer and distributor of products for the auto industry that primarily focuses on welding products and technology and is known as a Tier 2 manufacturer (the decision does not state where the Appellant is headquartered; the appeal was heard in Toronto, Ontario). It claimed SR&ED tax incentives under the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") for three resistance welding development projects in its tax return for the taxation year ending September 30, 2016, which is the only taxation year under appeal. The Minister of National Revenue denied the claim and the Appellant appealed; at the hearing, Jason Sousa of the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) testified, and Justice Graham found him credible but his evidence of little assistance. The appeal was heard under the Tax Court's informal procedure (Docket 2019-1422(IT)I) on November 24 and December 7, 2022, in Toronto, Ontario, before Justice David E. Graham; the Appellant was represented by its agent, Garry Siskos, and the decision records no adjournment request, medical certificate, or award of costs.

The substantive core of the dispute centred on whether the technical activities executed by JEC Distributors Inc.—three projects relating to its resistance welding products: Project 1, the "Data Link Flow Monitor" (sensors on each welding gun to monitor the flow and temperature of cooling water); Project 2, the "Anti-Fouling Chip Collector Improvement" (reliably collecting the copper chips produced when a dressing system resurfaces welding tips); and the project the parties referred to as Project 4, the "Method to Prevent Sealer Buildup on Dressing Blades"—satisfied the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. While the Appellant contended that its engineering efforts required overcoming complex technical obstacles to develop new and improved industrial products, the Crown, represented by counsel Chen Yu Zhang and Iris Kingston for the Respondent, maintained that the projects did not entail genuine technological risk or uncertainty and were instead resolved through routine engineering and standard industrial procedures. Applying the foundational jurisprudential framework set out in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (and rejecting the Appellant's reliance on Les Abeillies Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, which the Federal Court of Appeal essentially confined to its facts in R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 152), Justice Graham dismissed the appeal of the reassessment; because the parties agreed that only the first Northwest Hydraulic test was in issue, he found, for each of the three projects, that he was not satisfied there was technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures.
The Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

In Canada, the availability of R&D tax incentives is governed by a bifurcated statutory regime within the ITA that strictly separates technical eligibility from financial expenditure qualification. First, a taxpayer must demonstrate that the underlying technical activities conform to the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For commercial and industrial claimants, eligibility almost invariably rests on paragraph (c) of that definition, which encompasses experimental development—namely, work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Crucially, the statutory definition incorporates a strict boundary mechanism to prevent routine commercial operations from being subsidized through the tax system. Under paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1), work in respect of engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research is eligible only to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude a wide array of commercial and industrial activities from SR&ED eligibility, even where those activities are technically demanding or commercially innovative. These statutory exclusions encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

Once technical eligibility is established under subsection 248(1), the taxpayer may deduct current SR&ED expenditures (and add them to a cumulative carry-forward pool) pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the ITA, and claim Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) on "qualified expenditures" pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA. For a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), subsection 127(10.1) adds 20% to the 15% general rate, for an enhanced ITC rate of 35% on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's expenditure limit; under section 127.1, the enhanced credit earned on current expenditures is fully refundable for a qualifying corporation. Expenditures exceeding the limit earn the 15% general ITC under subsection 127(5), which is 40% refundable for a qualifying CCPC, while other corporations earn a 15% non-refundable ITC. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (Bill C-15), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, raised the expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million and extended the enhanced rate to eligible Canadian public corporations. However, pursuant to subsection 127(9) and the appellate jurisprudence affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178, upholding 2021 TCC 57), Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196), Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co. ([1987] 2 F.C. 60), and Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc. ([1996] F.C.J. No. 1226), any "government assistance" or "non-government assistance"—as well as contract payments received for performing SR&ED—must be deducted from the qualified expenditure pool, thereby preventing double subsidization of the same research outlay.

Because the statutory language of subsection 248(1) employs broad conceptual terms—such as "systematic investigation," "experiment or analysis," and "technological advancement"—Canadian courts evaluate technical eligibility through the mandatory five-question test articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC)). Under this sequential framework, the Court first asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, if such an uncertainty existed, the Court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the inquiry determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, and finally, the Court assesses whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.
Summary of the Tax Court of Canada's Final Holding

In JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170, the Tax Court of Canada applied the Northwest Hydraulic test and, because the parties agreed that only the first of its five tests was in issue, did not review the other four; it applied the first test to each of the three projects individually and held that each failed it. For Project 1, the Court accepted that the Appellant itself could not remove the technological risks and uncertainties through routine engineering or standard procedures, but held that the test is objective, not subjective: the Appellant had to show that the risks could not be overcome by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, and it offered no evidence on whether, for example, an electrical engineer, a skilled electrician, or a technician with networking expertise could have routinely solved the electrical noise and network connection problems. For Projects 2 and 4, the Court found that the Appellant had applied existing airflow and vacuum technology, rounded bin corners, and an existing anti-adhesive, atomizer and meter, which was a new use of existing technology and therefore routine engineering or standard procedures, and that there was no evidence that routine engineering or standard procedures could not have solved the remaining problem of the bin's size and weight. Because the first test of Northwest Hydraulic was not met and all five tests must be met, the appeal failed; the Court made no findings on hypotheses, scientific method, technological advancement, or record-keeping, and it did not consider the predictive-algorithm component of Project 1 because the Appellant never proceeded to that stage.

Furthermore, the decision forms part of a cohesive body of 2022–2023 Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence—alongside taxpayer losses in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 62), Gestion ACBK Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 94), 9158-1629 Québec Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 137), Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 127), and Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 35), and contrasted with taxpayer victories in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18) and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108)—that reinforces a strict judicial policing of the boundary between "technological advancement" and the mere "extension of existing technology" or "standard practice". Technical eligibility has remained under close judicial scrutiny in subsequent dockets, including taxpayer losses in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) and Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 129) and a taxpayer win in DAZZM Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129). The dismissal of JEC Distributors Inc.'s appeal underscores that product innovation, mechanical optimization, and commercial problem-solving do not qualify for SR&ED tax credits unless the taxpayer proves, objectively, that its technological uncertainty could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant fields; JEC Distributors Inc. lost on that point alone, even though the Court found its three employee witnesses (Joe Ruggiero, Paul Lichaa, and Bill Dodge) credible and their descriptions of the work very helpful.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

An authoritative examination of the ruling in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170, alongside the broader jurisprudential standards enforced by the Tax Court of Canada, shows that only one failure was decided in the case: the Appellant's failure to prove objective technological risk or uncertainty under the first Northwest Hydraulic test, which the parties agreed was the only test in issue (Failure 1 below). Failures 2 through 4 describe risks drawn from the broader jurisprudence and SR&ED practice; the Court in 2022 TCC 170 made no findings on them.
Failure 1: Conflation of Commercial and Engineering Complexity with Technological Uncertainty

The sole ground for the dismissal in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King was the Appellant's failure to establish "technological risk or uncertainty" under the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. In CRA administrative guidance (the phrasing below does not come from the reasons in 2022 TCC 170), technological uncertainty is commonly described as existing only when the probability of achieving a given technical objective or design specification cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. As Justice Bowman established in Northwest Hydraulic—and as the Tax Court applied in 2022 TCC 170, where Justice Graham stressed that the test is objective, not subjective—if the resolution of a technical problem is achievable by applying routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty, even where the taxpayer itself was unable to solve the problem.

The decision is better read as a failure of objective proof than as a finding that JEC Distributors Inc. confused difficulty with uncertainty: Justice Graham accepted that the Appellant itself could not remove the Project 1 risks, but held that it had not proved what competent professionals in other fields could have done. Taxpayers should nonetheless avoid conflating project uncertainty (or technical difficulty) with technological uncertainty. When an industrial firm designs new welding-cell equipment, such as sensors, chip collectors, or dressing-system accessories, or adapts manufacturing equipment, engineers inevitably encounter operational hurdles: components may not fit within spatial tolerances, materials may exhibit wear under cycle loads, or off-the-shelf subsystems may require calibration to operate in unison. However, uncertainty as to which existing engineering configuration will be most efficient, cost-effective, or reliable is not a technological uncertainty if the underlying physical, mechanical, or metallurgical principles governing each option are already well understood in the industry knowledge base.

In contrasting losses such as JEC Distributors Inc. (2022 TCC 170) and Mold Leaders Inc. (2023 TCC 127) with the taxpayer victory in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18), the decisive distinction lies in how the taxpayer defines "standard practice" and "system uncertainty". In Buhler Versatile, an agricultural equipment manufacturer in Winnipeg specializing in tractors successfully proved system uncertainty because combining the design features needed for high-horsepower 4WD tractors meeting Tier II emission standards created unpredictable interactions that could not be resolved by existing knowledge or standard procedures, which the taxpayer then systematically resolved following the five-question framework. Similarly, in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), a food manufacturer developing frozen pies demonstrated genuine technological uncertainty in balancing competing health and taste parameters beyond known formulation behaviour. Conversely, in JEC Distributors Inc., the Appellant, whose expertise was in welding technology, offered no evidence (such as testimony from an electrical engineer, a networking specialist, or a person knowledgeable about materials) that the electrical noise, contamination, communication protocol, or bin size-and-weight problems it encountered could not have been overcome by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in those fields. Consequently, the Court held that Project 1 did not meet the first test for lack of objective evidence, and that in Projects 2 and 4 the Appellant had made a new use of existing technology, which was still existing technology applied through routine engineering or standard procedures.
Failure 2: Absence of Hypothesis-Driven Experimentation (Trial-and-Error vs. Scientific Method)

Contrary to the suggestion that this was a second fatal deficiency, the Court in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King made no finding on whether the Appellant demonstrated a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"; because the parties agreed that only the first test was in issue, Justice Graham expressly declined to review the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. Under the Northwest Hydraulic interpretation of subsection 248(1), eligible experimental development must adhere to the total discipline of the scientific method. This requires a structured cognitive and operational sequence that begins with the rigorous observation and characterization of a technological limitation within the existing knowledge base, followed immediately by the formulation of a specific, causal hypothesis proposing why the phenomenon occurs and how a targeted manipulation of independent variables will resolve the technological uncertainty. The claimant must then design a controlled experiment or analytical model specifically structured to test the validity of that hypothesis, execute the testing protocol with systematic measurement and isolation of variables, and perform a rigorous analysis of the empirical data to accept, reject, or modify the hypothesis, thereby generating new technological knowledge.

In practice, many industrial claimants rely on empirical "trial-and-error" or iterative engineering optimization rather than systematic hypothesis testing. The factual narrative in JEC Distributors Inc. describes iterative work of this kind (testing different sensors and changing technologies until something seemed to work, trying 3D-printed and then machined aluminum bins, and adding an atomizer and then a flow meter), but the Court made no finding on whether that work met the second or third criteria. When an engineering team modifies a mechanical geometry, tests the prototype to see if it functions, observes a failure, and then adjusts another parameter until the device meets commercial specifications, they are engaging in standard iterative design. Without a clearly articulated a priori causal hypothesis linking the independent variable (such as alloy grain structure under specific thermal dissipation rates) to the dependent technological phenomenon, empirical testing merely evaluates product performance rather than testing a scientific or technological proposition. Paragraph 248(1)(f) of the ITA excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes, and testing that merely confirms whether a prototype works can fall within that exclusion; however, the Court in 2022 TCC 170 did not rely on paragraph 248(1)(f).
Failure 3: Confusing Product Development with Technological Advancement

Closely tied to technological uncertainty is the requirement to prove a "technological advancement" under the fourth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and paragraph 248(1)(c) of the ITA. A technological advancement is the generation of new information or knowledge that advances the general understanding of technology for competent professionals in the field. Although the Court in 2022 TCC 170 did not reach the fourth criterion, commentary reviewing JEC Distributors Inc. (2022 TCC 170), Dave's Diesel Inc. (2022 TCC 62), and Gestion ACBK Inc. (2022 TCC 94) together observes that taxpayers frequently confuse the creation of a new or improved product with the achievement of a technological advancement.

A product may be entirely novel in the marketplace, commercially superior to competitors' offerings, or even protected by industrial patents, yet involve zero technological advancement if it was constructed by combining and configuring known technologies in accordance with their known functional attributes. In JEC Distributors Inc., the Court made no finding on technological advancement; the reasons describe projects that ended without overcoming the problems (Project 1), with a bin that worked but was too big and heavy (Project 2), or with a successful spray system that customers would not buy because of health and safety costs (Project 4), but the decision turned only on the first test. Even in cases where a project fails commercially or technically, SR&ED eligibility can still be maintained if the failure generates new knowledge by proving that a hypothesized technological pathway is scientifically unviable, a principle established in Northwest Hydraulic and applied in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108). However, where the taxpayer merely applies standard engineering procedures to build a functional asset without advancing the underlying technological baseline, no SR&ED occurs.
Failure 4: Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation, Evidentiary Burden, and Expenditure Substantiation

The fourth area of risk, which was not a ground of decision in 2022 TCC 170, involves the evidentiary burden and the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic: the requirement to maintain detailed, dated records of hypotheses tested and experimental results as the work progressed. In Canadian tax litigation, the Minister's assumptions of fact in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal are presumed to be true until demolished by the taxpayer on a balance of probabilities, and appellate courts will not overturn a Tax Court judge's factual appreciation of the evidence absent a palpable and overriding error, as established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Housen v. Nikolaisen (2002 SCC 33). When the Minister assumes that a taxpayer's activities constituted routine engineering and lacked technological uncertainty, the taxpayer must lead evidence that objectively answers that assumption; in 2022 TCC 170 the Court found the Appellant's three employee witnesses credible and very helpful, yet their account of what the Appellant itself tried could not show what competent professionals in other fields could have achieved, and courts may likewise give little weight to ex post facto technical narratives drafted months or years after the taxation year by external SR&ED consultants.

In JEC Distributors Inc., the Court did not discuss the Appellant's documentation; the absence of contemporaneous records of hypotheses and systematic analysis has been a recurring theme in other 2022–2023 Tax Court losses, but it was not the basis of this decision. While the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic serves as an evidentiary weight indicator rather than an independent statutory condition in subsection 248(1), the Tax Court treats the lack of contemporaneous experimental records as powerful corroborative evidence that no systematic scientific investigation ever took place, echoing foundational principles from Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 D.T.C. 1363). Standard commercial records—such as purchase orders, final CAD drawings, invoices, and customer acceptance logs—prove only that a product was designed and built; they do not prove how or why specific experimental iterations were conducted to resolve a technological uncertainty.

Furthermore, from a financial and contractual standpoint, corporate claimants in the manufacturing and distribution sector face severe pitfalls regarding expenditure classification and contractual structuring under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA. As emphasized in recent stakeholder analyses of Tax Court jurisprudence, taxpayers—particularly Medical Professional Corporations (MPCs), Dental Professional Corporations (DPCs), and closely held industrial CCPC claimants—must rigorously distinguish between direct employee wages (which are eligible for the 55% proxy overhead method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA) and payments to arm's-length subcontractors or third parties (which are restricted to 80% ITC inclusion under subsection 127(9) and excluded from the proxy base). Without contemporaneous time-tracking records allocating employee hours specifically to eligible experimental activities (under paragraph 248(1)(d)) as opposed to commercial production, sales, or routine troubleshooting (excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k)), the entire salary claim is vulnerable to disallowance.

In addition, where a distributor or manufacturer develops custom equipment for a client or operates under intercompany licensing arrangements, ambiguous contract terms can trigger the "contract payment" or "funded research" exclusions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. If a customer pays for a custom machine or engineering solution, the CRA will deem the revenue to be a contract payment for SR&ED performed on behalf of another person unless the contract clearly establishes that the deliverable is a commercial good rather than SR&ED services, that the taxpayer retains ownership or controlling rights to the underlying foreground intellectual property, and that the taxpayer bears the full financial risk of technological failure. Similarly, any government or non-government assistance, forgivable loan, or non-commercial contribution must be netted against qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9), as strictly enforced by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178), where contributions paid to CAE under a Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative agreement (which CAE treated as loans) were held to be government assistance under subsection 127(9) because their terms, including an implicit rate of return significantly below market, were not those of an ordinary commercial agreement. In response, the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 (S.C. 2024, c. 17), assented to on June 20, 2024, excluded an "excluded loan" as defined in subsection 12(11) of the ITA (a non-forgivable loan evidenced in writing from a government, municipality or other public authority in Canada, for which bona fide arrangements were made for repayment within a reasonable time, and whose funds were used to earn income from a business or property) from the definition of government assistance, for loans made after December 31, 2019.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement governing SR&ED eligibility in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170, against what the Court actually decided in that case (only the first requirement was in issue) and the standard of proof demanded by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure or Court's Treatment in JEC Distributors Inc. (2022 TCC 170)
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: 1. Existence of Technological Risk or Uncertainty
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); Buhler Versatile Inc. (2023 TCC 18).

Failed to prove, objectively, that the technical challenges encountered could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field (no evidence from electrical, networking, or materials professionals); for Projects 2 and 4, the Court found a new use of existing technology. The Court accepted that the Appellant itself could not remove the Project 1 uncertainties, but held that this subjective inability was not enough.

Objective Knowledge Baseline: The taxpayer must establish the state of existing scientific/technological knowledge at project inception (via literature searches, patent reviews, or expert testimony) and prove that a competent professional could not predict whether the objective was achievable using standard practice.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); Canafric Inc. (2023 TCC 108).

Not in issue and not decided: the parties agreed that only the first test was in issue, so the Court did not review whether hypotheses were formulated. The reasons contain no finding that the Appellant stated project objectives as hypotheses.

Causal Proposition: A valid hypothesis must be an a priori testable statement correlating independent technical variables with dependent physical/technological outcomes to explain why a technological barrier exists and how it can be overcome.
3. Systematic Investigation via Experiment or Analysis
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3); Dave's Diesel Inc. (2022 TCC 62); Mold Leaders Inc. (2023 TCC 127).

Not in issue and not decided: the Court did not review the third test; its factual narrative describes iterative trials (different sensors, 3D-printed and aluminum bins, an atomizer and meter) without assessing them against the scientific method.

Total Discipline of the Scientific Method: The taxpayer must prove a systematic progression of experimental design, variable isolation, quantitative measurement, and analytical evaluation linking test results directly back to the modification or validation of the hypothesis.
4. Achievement of Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Gestion ACBK Inc. (2022 TCC 94); 9158-1629 Québec Inc. (2022 TCC 137).

Not in issue and not decided: the Court did not review the fourth test, although when applying the first test it described Projects 2 and 4 as a new use of existing technology. No finding was made on whether new technological knowledge was generated.

Advancement of Underlying Knowledge Base: Must demonstrate that the investigation yielded new, generalizable scientific or technological knowledge (even if the physical prototype failed) that advances the baseline understanding of skilled practitioners beyond standard practice.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation & Record-Keeping
ITA s. 230(1), s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); Sass Manufacturing Ltd. (88 D.T.C. 1363).

Not in issue and not decided: the Court did not review the fifth test or comment on the Appellant's records, so the reasons do not show whether it kept detailed, dated records created as the work progressed showing the hypotheses formulated, parameters tested, and analytical conclusions drawn. The Appellant's case rested on oral testimony from three employees, which the Court found credible and very helpful.

Contemporaneous Audit Trail: While not an absolute statutory bar in isolation, contemporaneous lab notes, test matrices, failure logs, and dated analytical reports are practically indispensable to corroborate oral testimony and demolish the Minister's assumptions of routine engineering.
6. Separation of Eligible Support Work & Expenditure Substantiation
ITA s. 37(1), s. 127(5), s. 127(9), s. 248(1)(d)–(k); CAE Inc. (2022 FCA 178).

Not in issue and not decided: the decision addresses only technological eligibility and contains no findings on separating routine engineering, commercial production, and quality control (s. 248(1)(f)/(i)) from eligible support work (s. 248(1)(d)). Wage versus third-party contractor allocation is a general risk, not an issue raised in this appeal.

Granular Nexus & Financial Rigour: Every claimed dollar of salary, material (consumed/transformed), or subcontractor outlay must be directly linked via contemporaneous time-tracking and project accounting to specific eligible experimental activities, net of assistance and contract payments.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To provide actionable legal and technical guidance for Canadian corporations and tax practitioners, the following two applied case studies model hypothetical industrial projects that exhibit the vulnerability penalized in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170. The vulnerability actually decided in that case was the failure to prove, objectively, that routine engineering or standard procedures could not resolve the uncertainty; the case studies also address other risks drawn from broader SR&ED jurisprudence and practice. For each scenario, a comprehensive, four-pillar remediation blueprint demonstrates step-by-step how to restructure project governance, technical documentation, contractual arrangements, and experimentation tracking to satisfy the Tax Court of Canada's strict evidentiary standards.
Case Study 1: Automated High-Speed Metallurgical Sample Preparation and Electrode Dressing Apparatus (Advanced Manufacturing & Industrial Tooling Sector)
Project Scenario & The "JEC Distributors" Pitfall

Consider "OntaWeld Precision Systems Inc." ("OntaWeld"), a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation based in Burlington, Ontario, that manufactures and distributes automated resistance spot-welding (RSW) electrode tip dressers and high-speed metallurgical sample preparation cutters used in automotive assembly lines. During the taxation year, automotive OEM clients transition to ultra-high-strength boron steel (UHSS) coated with an aluminum-silicon (Al-Si) layer. During spot welding, the molten Al-Si coating alloys with the copper-chromium-zirconium (CuCrZr) welding electrodes, causing rapid tip mushrooming, brittle intermetallic layer buildup, and micro-fissures. Simultaneously, OntaWeld is asked by an automotive client to supply a dual-blade rotary cutter and automated sample preparation unit that can mill away the contaminated intermetallic layer in under 1.2 seconds without inducing work-hardening or thermal micro-cracking in the underlying CuCrZr substrate, while preparing cross-sectional weld-nugget samples for optical measurement.

In its initial, un-restructured execution, OntaWeld's engineers design four successive cutter blade geometries using CAD software, outsource the machining of tungsten-carbide inserts to a local tool shop, and test them on a shop-floor welding robot until they find a rake angle and spindle speed (1,800 RPM) that achieves a clean cut in 1.15 seconds. In its T661 SR&ED claim, OntaWeld describes the technological uncertainty as "uncertainty whether a cutter blade could be designed to dress Al-Si contaminated electrodes and prepare weld samples in under 1.2 seconds without chattering." Upon audit, the CRA disallows 100% of the claim, citing JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 170) and Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 127), concluding that selecting cutting angles, testing carbide grades, and adjusting spindle RPMs constitute routine mechanical engineering and standard machining practice rather than addressing a genuine technological risk or uncertainty.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance & Defining the Baseline of Standard Practice

To survive judicial scrutiny under Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic, OntaWeld must institute a formal SR&ED Gate-Review Governance Protocol before any CAD design or metal-cutting begins. Under this governance structure, the Lead Metallurgical Engineer must first compile a dated State-of-the-Art & Standard Practice Dossier that establishes the objective knowledge baseline. This dossier records a comprehensive review of ASM International handbooks, cutting-tool manufacturer specifications for CuCrZr alloys, and peer-reviewed metallurgical literature on Al-Si intermetallic phases (Fe2Al5 and FeAl3).

With the baseline documented, the governance charter must explicitly separate the commercial objective (achieving a 1.2-second inline cycle time) from the underlying technological uncertainty. The dossier demonstrates that standard machining formulas dictate a low surface speed (< 150 m/min) with flood coolant to prevent galling and adhesive wear of ductile copper, whereas fracturing the hard, brittle Fe2Al5 intermetallic crust (> 800 HV hardness) in dry, inline robotic environments requires high shear-strain rates (> 450 m/min). At these elevated strain rates, existing tribological models cannot predict how adiabatic shear-band formation at the brittle-to-ductile interface (Fe2Al5 crust to CuCrZr core) will behave. This creates a fundamental scientific conflict: cutting parameters sufficient to shear the intermetallic crust without chipping the carbide edge induce subsurface plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization in the copper core, destroying its electrical conductivity. By documenting this conflict at inception, and by being prepared to prove it at trial with independent evidence from competent metallurgy and machining professionals (the type of objective evidence whose absence was decisive in JEC Distributors Inc.), OntaWeld can establish an objective system and metallurgical uncertainty that cannot be resolved by routine tooling selection or standard procedures.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation & Hypothesis Formulation

Instead of documenting commercial design iterations ("Version 1, Version 2, Version 3") or general product characterization, OntaWeld must restructure its technical documentation around explicit, causal scientific hypotheses to satisfy Criterion 2 of Northwest Hydraulic. Prior to fabricating any test inserts, the engineering team records Hypothesis H-01 in the formal project repository: it is hypothesized that introducing a variable-helix micro-chamfered chip-breaker (featuring a −12° primary negative land transitioning to a +22° positive shear rake) coated with a nanocomposite AlTiN/Si3N4 physical vapour deposition (PVD) layer will induce localized brittle fracture in the Fe2Al5 intermetallic layer via compressive stress waves while transitioning to low-friction adiabatic shearing in the CuCrZr substrate, thereby maintaining the interface temperature below the 450°C dynamic recrystallization threshold of CuCrZr at dry cutting speeds of 480 m/min. Furthermore, in strict compliance with paragraph 248(1)(d) and paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i) of the ITA, the technical documentation explicitly carves out the design of the pneumatic mounting bracket, protective housing, and PLC wiring as non-eligible routine engineering, claiming only the metallurgical modelling, experimental insert geometry fabrication, and tribological analysis directly commensurate with testing Hypothesis H-01.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Terms & Expenditure Qualification

To prevent financial disqualification or clawback under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, OntaWeld's tax counsel must restructure its commercial and subcontractor contracts prior to execution. First, to avoid the "contract payment" exclusion under subsection 127(9), the supply agreement with the automotive OEM must be drafted as a standard commercial Agreement for the Sale of Goods for a fixed price per delivered dressing unit, rather than a custom engineering or R&D services contract. The agreement must contain explicit legal covenants stipulating that OntaWeld is not contracted to perform SR&ED on behalf of the OEM, that customer payment is strictly contingent upon the delivery of a commercial apparatus meeting functional cycle-time specifications, that OntaWeld bears 100% of the financial risk of experimental failure, and that all foreground intellectual property, metallurgical datasets, and resulting patents vest exclusively in OntaWeld (or an affiliated Canadian IP holding entity with exclusive rights, avoiding the standing and licensing ambiguities seen in cross-border patent disputes).

Second, to substantiate third-party payments versus wages as emphasized in recent SR&ED jurisprudence, OntaWeld must overhaul its subcontractor Statements of Work (SOWs). When OntaWeld engages the local tool shop to grind experimental tungsten-carbide inserts, a generic invoice stating "Machining 20 cutter blades - $18,000" will be rejected by the CRA as a commercial purchase of capital or production goods. The SOW and invoice must be restructured to specify that the subcontractor is performing custom experimental fabrication of non-commercial test coupons (Insert Batches A1 through A4 with varying micro-chamfer angles) directly in support of OntaWeld's SR&ED project, that the work is performed wholly within Canada by an arm's-length Canadian resident contractor, and that the experimental inserts possess no commercial value and will be destructively tested during scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis, thereby qualifying the consumed material costs under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and the contractor fee at 80% for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9).
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking & Contemporaneous Record-Keeping

To satisfy Criterion 3 and Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic, OntaWeld replaces informal shop-floor trials with a controlled experimental matrix and contemporaneous laboratory log that records variable isolation, quantitative measurements, and analytical conclusions as the work progresses.

Case Study 2: Edge-Computing Acoustic Telemetry and Multi-Sensor Fusion in High-EMI Industrial Environments (Industrial IoT & Embedded Systems Sector)
Project Scenario & The "JEC Distributors" Pitfall

Consider "VectraSense Telemetry Corp." ("VectraSense"), an Ontario corporation that distributes and integrates industrial predictive-maintenance sensors for heavy stamping presses and automated manufacturing lines. VectraSense undertakes a project to develop an embedded edge-computing firmware module that fuses ultrasonic acoustic emission (100 kHz – 400 kHz) and triaxial MEMS accelerometer data to detect microscopic bearing spalling and hydraulic valve cavitation in real time on an active 2,000-ton stamping press. Because the stamping press generates intense electromagnetic interference (EMI) from high-current variable-frequency drives (VFDs) and massive mechanical shock waves during each stamping stroke, standard Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Kalman filtering algorithms running on an ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller suffer from severe signal aliasing, false-positive saturation (exceeding 65% false alarms), and memory buffer overflows due to the 1 MHz sampling rate required for ultrasonic signals.

In its initial, un-restructured execution, VectraSense's software developers download open-source C++ wavelet libraries, tweak filter coefficients, test different commercial Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) sampling rates, and refactor memory pointers until the firmware runs without crashing and false positives drop below 5%. In its SR&ED filing, VectraSense claims all software development hours across 14 months, describing the project as "developing a novel IoT edge firmware architecture to filter noisy sensor data on an embedded microcontroller." Upon review, the CRA denies the claim in full, citing JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 170), Gestion ACBK Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 94), and 9158-1629 Québec Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC 137). The CRA concludes that configuring open-source libraries, tuning filter parameters, and optimizing memory allocation constitute standard software engineering, routine debugging, and an application of existing digital signal processing (DSP) technology rather than a systematic investigation overcoming technological uncertainty.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance & Defining Algorithmic and System Uncertainty

To overcome the "routine engineering or standard procedures" characterization applied in JEC Distributors Inc. and related Tax Court jurisprudence, VectraSense must institute a formal Technical Architecture & Algorithmic Baseline Review prior to writing any code. The Chief Systems Architect compiles a dated baseline mathematical analysis demonstrating why standard signal processing techniques available in the public domain objectively fail under these operating conditions. Specifically, the baseline review proves that while Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT) can isolate non-stationary transient cavitation spikes from non-Gaussian EMI noise, they require 𝒪(N2) floating-point operations per window, exceeding the deterministic real-time compute ceiling (< 2 ms latency) and 512 KB SRAM limit of the Cortex-M7 architecture by a factor of 8.4×. Conversely, while Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) with fixed dyadic decimation operate within 𝒪(N) time complexity, they exhibit severe shift-variance: whenever a high-energy mechanical stamping shock wave coincides with an ultrasonic cavitation burst, phase distortion across decimation levels obliterates the high-frequency cavitation signature.

Through this formal review, the project governance charter defines the barrier not as "making the firmware work," but as an objective algorithmic and resource-constrained system uncertainty: whether a shift-invariant, non-linear time-frequency decomposition algorithm can be mathematically constructed within an 𝒪(N log N) integer-quantized computational complexity bound without losing phase coherence in the 150 kHz – 350 kHz ultrasonic band when subjected to simultaneous broadband electromagnetic impulse noise (> 40 dB SNR degradation) and mechanical shock harmonics. This framing, supported where necessary by independent evidence from competent DSP and embedded-systems professionals (JEC Distributors Inc. failed because it offered no evidence of what electrical or networking professionals could have done about electrical noise and network connections on a resistance welding line), positions the project as eligible experimental development under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation & Hypothesis Formulation

VectraSense next restructures its software engineering documentation to strictly segregate routine system development—such as user-interface dashboards, MQTT cloud telemetry protocols, printed circuit board (PCB) layout, and standard peripheral driver integration—from the core experimental DSP kernel. Before creating any experimental code branches, the research team formulates and logs Hypothesis DSP-H1: it is hypothesized that replacing standard dyadic DWT filter banks with an adaptive, dual-tree complex wavelet packet transform (DT-CWPT) utilizing lifting-scheme integer arithmetic and dynamic entropy-based pruning coupled to the triaxial accelerometer's zero-crossing phase reference will preserve shift-invariance within ±3° phase error and suppress VFD electromagnetic impulse noise by > 32 dB, while bounding worst-case execution time (WCET) to < 1.6 ms and SRAM consumption to < 180 KB. The technical file incorporates mathematical proofs, Python/MATLAB theoretical simulation benchmarks, and exact quantitative failure thresholds so that every subsequent firmware iteration tests a specific mathematical variable in Hypothesis DSP-H1 rather than performing unguided debugging.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Terms, Government Assistance, and IP Governance

Because software and Industrial IoT companies frequently utilize government innovation funding—such as NRC IRAP, provincial innovation grants, or federal strategic loans—and rely on specialized technical personnel, VectraSense's legal counsel implements three critical contractual and financial safeguards. First, counsel audits all government funding agreements under subsection 127(9) of the ITA in light of the Federal Court of Appeal's binding precedent in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178). In CAE Inc., the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the Tax Court's finding that contributions paid under a Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative agreement, on terms that did not reflect an ordinary commercial agreement, constitute "government assistance" within the meaning of subsection 127(9), which reduces the company's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool for ITC purposes and must also be included in taxable income. Since the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1, however, a bona fide repayable "excluded loan" within the meaning of subsection 12(11) of the ITA made after December 31, 2019 is not government assistance, so counsel first determines whether each loan meets that definition. Consequently, if VectraSense receives a $150,000 government contribution or low-interest conditional loan, tax counsel structures the financing agreement and internal cost-accounting ledgers so that the funding is explicitly allocated toward non-SR&ED commercial activities (such as market readiness, UI development, UL/CE certification, or commercial field deployment), or, to the extent it funds the DSP research, is transparently deducted from the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool on Form T661 to prevent reassessment penalties. Furthermore, where VectraSense leverages complementary Canadian intellectual property incentives—such as the Quebec Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) patent box, IP Ontario (IPON), IRAP IP Assist, or Elevate IP—counsel ensures that legal expenses for patent drafting and prosecution are segregated from section 37 SR&ED expenditures, as patent filing costs are excluded from SR&ED eligibility.

Second, counsel addresses the remuneration rules governing "specified employees" (shareholders owning 10% or more of any class of shares of the corporation or a related corporation) versus arm's-length third-party consultants. Because subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1) of the ITA prohibit claiming bonuses paid to specified employees and cap their eligible SR&ED salary at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), VectraSense restructures its Lead Architect's compensation prior to the fiscal year into regular, fixed T4 base salary rather than performance bonuses, while ensuring that external DSP specialists are engaged under Canadian-resident subcontractor agreements with explicit SR&ED Statements of Work. Third, when VectraSense installs sensor prototypes on a client's 2,000-ton stamping press to capture empirical EMI and vibration datasets, the arrangement is governed by a formal No-Cost Experimental Field-Trial & Site Access Agreement rather than a commercial lease or sale. This contract stipulates that title to the prototype hardware remains exclusively with VectraSense, no commercial consideration is paid by the host facility, and the sole purpose of the site access is to execute experimental testing protocols to validate Hypothesis DSP-H1.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking & Contemporaneous Record-Keeping

In software and embedded systems claims, the Tax Court of Canada routinely rejects generic issue-tracking tickets ("Fix memory leak in buffer," "Update filter module") as evidence of routine software engineering. To satisfy Criteria 3 and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic, VectraSense integrates its Git version-control repository and project management workflow directly into a contemporaneous SR&ED experimental tracking matrix. All experimental code is isolated in a dedicated repository branch (sred/dt-cwpt-lifting-experiments), and every commit message is required to reference a specific Hypothesis ID and Experiment ID, detailing the mathematical parameter modified, the empirical benchmark result, and the analytical conclusion.

All subsequent engineering hours spent porting the validated v0.6-exp3 kernel into the commercial production firmware release (main/prod-v1.0) are automatically classified as non-eligible commercial production activities under paragraph 248(1)(i) of the ITA.
5. Synthesis of Strategic Takeaways for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170, serves as an unmistakable warning to Canadian industrial, manufacturing, and technology enterprises: the statutory threshold for SR&ED eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act cannot be satisfied merely by demonstrating that a project was technically challenging, required multiple prototypes, or resulted in an innovative commercial product. Both the CRA and the Tax Court rigorously apply the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic as cumulative requirements, all of which must be met; in JEC Distributors Inc., the parties agreed that only the first was in issue, and the appeal failed because the Appellant did not prove, objectively, that its uncertainties could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.

To insulate SR&ED claims against audit disallowance and prevail in litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, legal counsel and technical advisors must transition their compliance methodology from retrospective claim writing to proactive, contemporaneous evidentiary engineering. By formally documenting the objective limits of standard practice at project inception (and, if a claim is litigated, proving those limits with independent evidence from competent professionals in every relevant discipline, the step missing in JEC Distributors Inc.), framing technical obstacles as causal scientific or technological hypotheses, executing controlled experiments with quantitative variable isolation, strictly segregating routine commercial engineering under paragraph 248(1)(d), and aligning subcontractor, customer, and government assistance agreements with subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, Canadian taxpayers can construct an authoritative evidentiary record capable of withstanding the strictest judicial scrutiny.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled the taxpayer failed to establish technological uncertainty or provide adequate supporting records.
